title: Topology-independent quantum advantage in communication networks
authors: Ankush Pandit, V. N. S. Meghanath Ashtakala, Leon George Padayatty, Debashis Saha
abstract: Quantum communication can outperform classical communication in a variety of information-processing tasks, but such advantages are typically established for a fixed communication network. Here we introduce topology-independent quantum advantage, in which a quantum protocol outperforms every classical protocol subject to the same communication constraint, irrespective of how the classical communication resource is distributed among the parties or which communication topology is employed, even when the parties may share unlimited classical randomness. We first demonstrate this phenomenon through a simple three-party equality task: two senders receive ternary classical inputs, while an input-free receiver determines whether the inputs are equal. We then formulate a general framework for topology-independent communication and completely characterize the corresponding classical correlation polytope in the minimal three-party scenario. Its facet inequalities reveal several instances of topology-independent quantum advantage. Remarkably, one of these inequalities enables the semi-device-independent certification of a nonunitary quantum channel, while another certifies a sequential quantum network topology without any prior assumption about the network configuration. Finally, we extend the framework to four-party networks, characterize the relevant classical communication structures, and identify a communication task exhibiting quantum advantages against all admissible classical topologies. Our results establish topology independence as a genuine and robust form of quantum advantage in communication networks.
summary: This work defines and proves the existence of 'topology-independent quantum advantage' in communication networks. It shows that quantum protocols can outperform all classical protocols even when the classical resource distribution or network topology is unknown. The findings provide a robust theoretical tool for certifying quantum advantages in communication systems.
main_problem: The paper introduces and rigorously investigates the concept of 'topology-independent quantum advantage' in quantum communication networks.
main_result: It establishes that quantum protocols can outperform all classical protocols subject to the same total communication constraint, regardless of the specific communication topology used.
method: The authors characterize the classical correlation polytope by considering the convex hull of correlations achievable across all possible admissible communication topologies (represented by DAGs).
model_or_system: The model involves $N$ sender parties and one receiver in a communication network. The advantage is tested by comparing quantum achievable rates against the maximum rate achievable by any classical strategy under a total communication resource constraint.
key_observables: The success rate of the protocol (e.g., $I_{quantum}$ vs $I_{classical}$), and specific information quantities like $I_5$ and $I_{12}$.
important_parameters: The total communication resource constraint ($d$), the number of parties ($N$), and the specific input/output alphabet sizes.
main_assumptions: The classical protocol is free to distribute the total communication resource among parties arbitrarily, and the analysis focuses on the total communication constraint rather than a fixed topology.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate various communication topologies (DAGs) used to characterize the classical correlation polytope, and the analysis uses tables to list facet inequalities.
paper_structure: The paper first demonstrates the concept in a simple three-party equality task, then develops a general framework using weighted DAGs to characterize the classical polytope, and finally extends the analysis to four-party networks.
why_interesting: The concept of topology-independent advantage provides a robust measure of quantum advantage that is independent of the physical layout of the communication network, which is highly relevant for designing practical quantum communication protocols.

FIG. 2: All communication topologies sufficient to characterize the topology-independent classical correlations in the [(3, 3, 3), 2, 6] scenario. The directed edges indicate the allowed communication channels, with the corresponding message dimensions indicated alongside the edges. (a) Here, i ∈{1, 2, 3}, resulting in 3 topologies. (b) Here, (i, j) represents all possible combinations from the set {1, 2, 3}, resulting in 6 distinct topologies. (c) Here, (i, j, k) represents all possible permutations from the set {1, 2, 3}, resulting in 6 topologies. (d) Here, i ∈{1, 2, 3}, with j and k being distinct from i and each other, resulting in 3 topologies.
